passages.t: Every firstborn belongs to the LORD
passages.happening: “Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Consecrate to Me every firstborn male. The firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast’” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
Israel has just walked out of Egypt. Before the story moves on, it pauses to make sure the night will never be forgotten.

The claim comes straight from chapter 12. Egypt's firstborn died. Israel's firstborn were spared, under the blood. So from now on they belong to the LORD in a special way. They are alive by mercy, not because they deserved it.

To ‘consecrate’ means to set apart for God. In the ancient world the firstborn son was the heir, the family's future, and firstborn animals and first harvests were often offered to the gods. Israel's law claims every firstborn for the LORD, but, as the next verses show, it refuses child sacrifice.
passages.later:
God later took the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn: “for all the firstborn are Mine. On the day I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated to Myself all the firstborn in Israel” (Numbers 3:13).

Luke tells how Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple “to present Him to the Lord”, because the law says, “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord” (Luke 2:22-23).
passages.hard:
Why does God claim the firstborn, and what about the firstborn of Egypt who died? The claim on Israel's firstborn follows straight from the death of Egypt's firstborn, and a reader can feel the weight of that.

The text presents that plague as judgment on a power that had enslaved Israel and ordered its baby boys killed (1:22), the end of a long contest in which Pharaoh refused again and again. The law here draws a lesson for Israel: its firstborn are alive by mercy, not merit, and so they belong to God.

Notice too what the chapter rules out. The LORD does not take Israel's children in sacrifice. He requires that they be bought back.

Readers still differ on how to weigh the deaths in Egypt: as God's just judgment on a nation's cruelty, as a hard part of an ancient account told in the language of its day, or some of both. The Bible itself speaks of it with seriousness, not triumph. The notes on Exodus 11 and 12 say more.
passages.asks: Israel's firstborn were alive by mercy, so they belonged to God. Ask what in your life you owe to God's mercy. And ask what it would mean to give that back to him, not as payment, but as thanks.

passages.happening:
“So Moses told the people, ‘Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; for the LORD brought you out of it by the strength of His hand. And nothing leavened shall be eaten’” (verse 3). “Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving” (verse 4).

When they come into the land, they are to keep this service in this month: seven days of unleavened bread, with a feast on the seventh (verses 5-7).

“And on that day you are to explain to your son, ‘This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ It shall be a sign for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead that the Law of the LORD is to be on your lips” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Abib is a word connected with ripening ears of grain. The month falls in the spring. After the exile it was called Nisan.

Two phrases come again and again in this chapter: ‘out of the house of slavery’ and ‘with a mighty hand’. They are like a short creed, a summary Israel was meant to say aloud.

Listen to what the parent says in verse 8: ‘what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt’. Not for our ancestors, but for me. Every generation was to speak as if it had come out of Egypt itself. The story is not only history. It is each person's own story.

The ‘sign for you on your hand’ and the ‘reminder on your forehead’ may have been meant as a picture, like a string tied round a finger. Jewish tradition came to keep it literally, in tefillin: small leather boxes holding passages of Scripture, this chapter among them, bound on the arm and the head for prayer. Examples have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Jesus mentions them.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy gives the same command about God's words: “Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads” (Deuteronomy 6:8).

Jesus mentions these boxes when he warns against religion done for show: “All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels” (Matthew 23:5). His point is not the boxes. It is the heart that wants to be seen.
passages.asks: The parent was to say, ‘what the LORD did for me’. Ask whether you can tell God's work in your own life in the first person, as your story. And ask who you could tell it to this week.

passages.happening:
When the LORD brings them into the land, “you are to present to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb” (verse 12). “You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you must redeem” (verse 13).

“In the future, when your son asks you, ‘What does this mean?’ you are to tell him, ‘With a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery’” (verse 14). “This is why I sacrifice to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
To ‘redeem’ means to buy back. Israel's sons are claimed by God, and then bought back. Later law set the price at five shekels of silver (Numbers 18:16). God never wanted Israel's children sacrificed. Child sacrifice was what other peoples' gods demanded. The LORD claims the child and gives the child back.

The donkey was not an animal used in sacrifice. So a firstborn donkey was bought back with a lamb, or else killed rather than kept.

Again a child asks a question, and again the parent tells the story. The rite raises the question; the story gives the answer. That is how faith was to be passed on in Israel's homes.
passages.later:
Israel's law later set the price: “five shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary shekel” (Numbers 18:16).

Peter turns the picture to Christ: “it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18-19). Paul calls Christ “the firstborn over all creation” (Colossians 1:15). The firstborn who was presented in the temple becomes the one who pays the price for others.
passages.asks: God claims the firstborn and then gives them back. Ask what you have that you feel God has a claim on: a child, a gift, a future. And ask whether you trust him enough to give it to him, knowing he is not like gods who devour what is given.

passages.t: The long way round, and Joseph's bones
passages.happening:
“When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter. For God said, ‘If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt’” (verse 17).

“So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle” (verse 18).

“Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, ‘God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place’” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The ‘road through the land of the Philistines’ was the main coast road from Egypt to Canaan, the shortest way. In this period Egypt guarded that road with a chain of forts. A column of runaway slaves would have met soldiers.

So God leads them the long way, because he knows his people. They are not ready for war. They might turn back. God's guidance takes account of their weakness. The shorter road is not always the better one.

The mention of the Philistines raises a question about dates. The Philistines settled on that coast around the 1100s BC. Some take the name as a later writer calling the road by what it was called in his own day. Others take it as a sign of a later date for the exodus. The book page sets out the views.

‘Red Sea’ is in Hebrew yam suph, sea of reeds. Where Israel crossed is discussed in the next chapter.

And Moses takes Joseph's bones. Genesis ended with Joseph's dying wish that his bones be carried home (Genesis 50:25). Centuries later, his family keeps the promise. Joseph's faith that God would bring them out is answered.
passages.later:
Joseph's oath is in Genesis: “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place” (Genesis 50:25). Hebrews honors his faith: “By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones” (Hebrews 11:22).

The bones finally rest in the land: “And the bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem” (Joshua 24:32).
passages.asks: God led Israel the long way round because they were not ready for battle. Ask whether God may be leading you by a longer road than you wanted, for your good. And ask what promise, like Joseph's bones, you are carrying toward a home you have not yet reached.

passages.t: The pillar of cloud and fire
passages.happening:
“They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness” (verse 20).

“And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night. Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people” (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
Succoth is often placed in the Wadi Tumilat, a valley leading east from the Delta. Where Etham was is not known. It lay ‘on the edge of the wilderness’.

Now God's presence goes before them in a form they can see. By day a pillar of cloud. By night a pillar of fire. They are not left to find their own way.

And it never leaves. ‘Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place.’ The same cloud will later cover the tabernacle and fill it with God's glory (40:34-38). The God who came down to rescue now walks ahead of his people.
passages.later:
Israel remembered: “You led them with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they should travel” (Nehemiah 9:12). “He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night” (Psalm 78:14).

The cloud rests on the tabernacle in Numbers: “the cloud would cover the tabernacle by day, and at night it would appear like fire” (Numbers 9:16). And Paul writes that “our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1).
passages.asks: The pillar never left its place before the people. Ask where you need God to go before you right now. And ask what it would mean to follow, step by step, rather than to see the whole road first.
